name: JSON BinPack
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers)
workload: Encoded size of 400+ real-world JSON documents (SchemaStore test suite, 36-category taxonomy) compared across 12+ binary serialization formats, schema-driven and schema-less.
claimed_speedup: JSON BinPack is as space-efficient or more space-efficient than every one of 12+ alternative formats tested in every considered case; e.g. ESLint config sample: 64 bytes vs 1,141 bytes JSON (~94% reduction); also typically beats GZIP/LZMA/LZ4 at max compression for small/medium documents.
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed (AGPL-3.0-or-later or paid commercial license) — AGPL's network-copyleft is a real adoption barrier for closed-source SaaS use. Space-efficiency focused, not runtime-efficiency focused; project's own FAQ recommends FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto instead when zero-copy runtime speed matters. Requires JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions for schema-driven mode.
caveats: Compiler flags and hardware/CPU model for the benchmark run are not published, so it falls short of Tier A despite being methodologically rigorous (peer-examined MSc dissertation at Oxford, CAR Hoare prize, arXiv preprints 2201.02089/2201.03051/2211.12799, public benchmark code and raw results). Benchmark measures encoded byte size, not wall-clock throughput/latency, against protobuf/capnp/flatbuffers/msgpack reference implementations.

name: rkyv
baseline: Cap'n Proto, FlatBuffers, Protocol Buffers (via prost/protobuf crates), MessagePack (via rmp-serde/msgpacker/zerompk)
workload: Serialize/deserialize/zero-copy-access speed and size on structured Rust datasets (HTTP log records, 3D mesh data, Minecraft save data) via Criterion benchmarks in the independently-hosted rust_serialization_benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: On the 'log' dataset: rkyv serialize 178.87 µs vs FlatBuffers 763.63 µs (~4.3x faster) and vs Cap'n Proto 480.15 µs (~2.7x faster); rkyv unvalidated zero-copy access ~1.09 ns and unvalidated deserialize 8.33 µs vs FlatBuffers unvalidated access 2.18 ns / deserialize 42.2 µs. Results are workload-dependent: on 'minecraft_savedata' and other datasets rkyv trails the fastest library (e.g. ~38-54% of best relative serialize speed).
hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs (Hyper-V virtualized), x86_64
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no official C API, so not directly usable from C++ (qualifies under the 'non-C++ implementations welcome' rule). Zero-copy access model requires careful handling of untrusted input (validation feature adds cost, shown separately in the 'validated upfront with error' benchmark rows). Not a schema/IDL system like Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers/Protobuf — Rust-type-driven instead.
caveats: Benchmark repo (rust_serialization_benchmark) is maintained by rkyv's own author plus collaborators, not a fully independent third party, though it is public, reproducible, and covers dozens of competing libraries fairly. Original rkyv-authored blog post 'rkyv is faster than...' is now a dead/redirected domain, so this entry relies on the maintained benchmark repo instead. Relative performance varies significantly by dataset/workload.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20flatbuffers -> 'Rkyv is faster than {bincode, capnp, cbor, flatbuffers, postcard, prost}' -> github.com/rkyv/rkyv -> github.com/djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark

name: Quarry
workload: Encode/decode ops-per-second and bytes-per-record for telemetry and large-payload workloads, comparing Quarry's C and C++ generated code (BRF wire format) against protoc-generated Protobuf C++ (default and Arena) code, five aggregated CI runs.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, honestly reported: Protobuf wins telemetry encode/decode (18.81M/13.48M ops/s vs Quarry C 9.69M/5.45M) and large encode (1.60M vs 0.48M), but Quarry C wins large-payload decode (0.85M ops/s vs Protobuf C++ 0.57M and Protobuf Arena 0.45M, ~1.5-1.9x faster). Quarry's BRF format is larger on the wire than Protobuf in the tested cases (e.g. 60 vs 16 bytes/record for telemetry).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763, Linux/x86_64 GitHub-hosted CI runner
tradeoffs: Header-only/deterministic-footprint native runtime (claimed zero native runtime size) vs Protobuf's external runtime library. Larger wire format than Protobuf on tested workloads. Very new/low-adoption project; README explicitly warns shared-runner timing is 'informational' and depends on hardware/compiler/optimization/runtime/workload.
caveats: Extremely low star count (4) and single-maintainer project; only a narrow win (large-payload decode) rather than an across-the-board win — reported honestly per instructions rather than cherry-picked. GitHub Actions shared runners add benchmark noise, acknowledged by the author.
found_via: gh search repos "binary serialization" language:C++ --sort stars -> ip332/quarry

name: Karmem
workload: Go benchmark (testing/benchmark) encode/decode of an object-API generated struct, both native (Go) and inside WebAssembly (Wazero runtime), on Apple M1 hardware.
claimed_speedup: Karmem ~10x faster than FlatBuffers: native EncodeObjectAPI 0.51ms vs 2.54ms (-79.85%), DecodeObjectAPI 0.20ms vs 3.57ms (-94.30%); inside WASM/Wazero EncodeObjectAPI 4.0ms vs 17.2ms (-76.51%), DecodeObjectAPI 1.9ms vs 50.7ms (-96.18%). Also zero allocations vs FlatBuffers' allocations per op.
compiler_and_flags: Go compiler (version unstated), go test -bench with benchstat comparison
tradeoffs: Designed primarily for WebAssembly host/guest data sharing (TinyGo/WASM), not general-purpose RPC; author states FlatBuffers 'causes panics due to lack of bound-checking' motivating the project. No Rust/C++ note beyond Go/TinyGo/AssemblyScript targets claimed in docs.
caveats: Repo has had no commits since March 2023 (>3 years), so it is abandoned despite the strong numbers; Go compiler version and optimization flags are not stated in the benchmark output, capping this below Tier A.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20flatbuffers -> 'Karmem: A fast binary serialization format faster than Google Flatbuffers' -> github.com/inkeliz/karmem

name: qdf (Quick Data Format)
workload: Wire size and allocations for batches of realistic structured records (OTLP traces, logs, RTB bids, events, IoT float series) encoded record-for-record by json/msgpack/protobuf/flatbuffers/qdf on the same fixtures, via a reproducible `scripts/compare.sh` benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: qdf smaller than Protobuf on every one of 5 batch fixtures at the compression tier: RTB -38%, IoT -29%, OTLP -68%, Logs -60%, Events -39% (up to 68% smaller than Protobuf per README). On a 5,000-row Active-Directory export, qdf OptBalanced is 2.1x smaller and 2.1x faster to encode and ~7x faster to decode than encoding/json, ~1.8x smaller/~2x faster to decode than msgpack. Author honestly notes FlatBuffers still wins raw encode-allocation and single-tiny-message size, and Protobuf/FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26, default build, benchmark suite in bench/ module run with `-count=6`
tradeoffs: Go-only, pure-Go, no schema/IDL (struct-tag based, alpha format that 'still moves'). Wins are on batches with cross-record repetition; single tiny messages favor Protobuf/FlatBuffers per author's own comparison. Compression tier trades encode CPU for size (e.g. ~70 MB/s vs ~1100 MB/s for the balanced tier on float data).
caveats: Small project (26 stars), alpha status, format not yet frozen. Benchmark hardware is a single named laptop CPU rather than a controlled server; author explicitly flags this ('speed numbers are machine-specific').
found_via: gh search repos topic:binary-serialization --sort stars -> alex60217101990/qdf

name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x faster) and vs MessagePack 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x faster); BebopMessage 231.7 ns similarly ~4.5x faster than Protobuf. Repo README states Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization' among the tested formats, and Protobuf becomes 'the slowest of the binary serializers' on deserialization.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical / 16 physical cores, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: The independent benchmark repo (ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks) is small (6 stars) and was last updated in 2021, so it predates recent Bebop/Protobuf/.NET releases; results may not reflect current versions. It is however a genuinely third-party, non-Bebop-affiliated benchmark with full BenchmarkDotNet environment info published, and Bebop's own docs/HN discussion corroborate a large speed advantage over Protobuf.
found_via: WebSearch: query='Bebop serialization benchmark faster than protobuf flatbuffers github' -> github.com/ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks

name: fernBuffer
workload: Encoded byte size of 10 representative JSON-like payloads (logs, flat records, hex strings, sparse nulls, repeated strings, float/int/bool arrays, tiny objects, deep nesting) encoded by fernBuffer vs Python's msgpack library.
claimed_speedup: Smaller than MessagePack on 7 of 10 test cases, e.g. log entries 10.9 KB vs 15.1 KB (~28% smaller), sparse nulls 903 B vs 1.9 KB (~52% smaller), repeated strings 557 B vs 1.2 KB (~54% smaller); but larger than MessagePack on float array, int array, bool array, and tiny objects cases.
tradeoffs: Author explicitly labels it 'more of a prototype / proof of concept ... bugs or flaws may exist'. C library with a small C API (usable from C++), also exposes a ctypes-based Python binding. No zero-copy/schema features.
caveats: No compiler/hardware stated for the size-only benchmark; results are honestly mixed (worse than MessagePack on 3-4 of 10 cases, per the project's own table). Tiny, single-author, very new project.
found_via: gh search repos "binary serialization" language:C++ --sort stars -> Escartem/fernBuffer

name: MTS-1 (Lightweight Delta-Encoded Telemetry Format)
workload: Synthetic telemetry payload size comparison (storage footprint) of MTS-1 against JSON, JSON Lines, CBOR, MessagePack, and Protocol Buffers for low-resource/offline-first system health monitoring.
claimed_speedup: Reported ~5.4% smaller than MessagePack and 74.6-74.7% smaller than JSON on the paper's synthetic S1 dataset (MTS-1 1.39 MB vs MessagePack 1.47 MB). Protocol Buffers was explicitly excluded from quantitative testing by the authors ('schema compilation requirements incompatible with dynamic monitoring scenarios').
tradeoffs: No throughput/latency numbers at all, only payload size; Protobuf, one of the category's core baselines, was deliberately not benchmarked. No implementation language, code repository, or reference implementation could be found.
caveats: No code repository found for MTS-1; this is a January 2026 arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), single-author, with only synthetic benchmarking and no production validation, and a fairly modest (5.4%) win over MessagePack. Included as a paper-only research-section entry per instructions since it directly compares against a baseline in the target list.
found_via: arXiv: search_query=abs:%22Protocol+Buffers%22+AND+abs:%22performance%22 -> arXiv:2601.01602 'MTS-1: A Lightweight Delta-Encoded Telemetry Format...'

name: greenpack
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal microbenchmarks of a fixed struct (name, birthday, phone, siblings, spouse, money) across ~20 Go serialization libraries, using Go's testing/benchmark tool, in the companion go_serialization_benchmarks shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: README states greenpack reads are 6% faster and writes 15% faster than Gogoprotobuf-based Protocol Buffers, with zero allocation on write (Gogoprotobuf allocates). Raw shootout numbers: GreenPackMarshal 129 ns/op (0 B/op) vs GogoprotobufMarshal 152 ns/op (64 B/op) and vs ProtobufMarshal 936 ns/op (200 B/op).
tradeoffs: Pure Go, code-generation based (like msgp/msgpack), msgpack2-compatible wire format for cross-language interoperability. Modest win margin (6-15%) over Protobuf, not a dramatic speedup; author explicitly notes ZebraPack and CapNProto/Gencode can be faster in some cases.
caveats: The specific comparison numbers come from the go_serialization_benchmarks suite, last updated 2017 with a beta-era Go compiler (1.8beta2) on old hardware — results are dated and margins this small could shift with modern Go/Protobuf versions. greenpack itself remains actively maintained (2026 commits).
found_via: gh search repos "faster than protobuf" --sort stars -> glycerine/greenpack

name: ZebraPack
workload: Same go_serialization_benchmarks shootout: Marshal/Unmarshal microbenchmarks of a fixed struct across ~20 Go serialization libraries using Go's testing/benchmark tool.
claimed_speedup: Fastest marshal (write) of all tested libraries in the shootout: ZebraPackMarshal 120 ns/op (0 B/op) vs GoprotobufMarshal 500 ns/op (~4.2x faster), ProtobufMarshal 936 ns/op (~7.8x faster), CapNProtoMarshal 498 ns/op (~4.2x faster), and FlatBufferMarshal 379 ns/op (~3.2x faster). Also 0 B/op allocation on marshal.
tradeoffs: Author's own README says use greenpack instead now ('a more recent alternative'). Go-only, code-generation based like msgp, msgpack2-compatible wire format for other-language interop.
caveats: Harvested as the top marshal-speed winner from the go_serialization_benchmarks shootout per 'harvest the winners' instruction. Explicitly superseded by greenpack and unmaintained since 2018 (>3 years, abandoned); benchmark data is from 2017 on an old Go beta compiler, so absolute numbers are stale even though the repo/data are public and reproducible.
found_via: gh search repos "faster than protobuf" -> glycerine/greenpack README references [1] go_serialization_benchmarks -> harvested ZebraPack as the shootout's marshal-speed winner

name: HyperSerializer
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize+deserialize of 1,000,000 instances of a 10-field 'Test' class (Guid, int, long, DateTime, uint, decimal, TimeSpan, enum, string), comparing HyperSerializer, MessagePack, Protobuf, and ApexSerializer.
claimed_speedup: README states HyperSerializer is 'up to 16x faster than MessagePack and Protobuf, and 2x faster than MemoryPack' with roughly equivalent or better memory allocation; elsewhere states 'roughly 3x faster than ApexSerializer and 18x faster than MessagePack and Protobuf'.
tradeoffs: Contract-less: relies on identical field/property layout between source and destination types, no versioning/schema-evolution support; mismatched types can throw or silently misdecode. .NET only, span-based, described by its author as a 'champion/challenger (C++ vs C#) experiment'.
caveats: Benchmark numbers are presented only as PNG charts in the README (Time.png / Space.png), not as a text table, and no CPU model or BenchmarkDotNet environment block is published in visible README text, so this is capped at Tier C despite using BenchmarkDotNet internally. The two stated ratios (16x vs 18x) are also inconsistent between sections of the same README.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20protobuf -> gh search repos "faster than protobuf" --sort stars -> adam-dot-cohen/HyperSerializer
